GSTR-2B

Credit is only what your supplier filed.

This matches your purchase register line by line against the GSTR-2B the government built from your suppliers' filings, sorts every row into five categories, scores the near-matches, and leads with one number: the credit at risk, in rupees. It works from a file you downloaded — the portal JSON or the Excel export — and we never hold your GSTN credentials or log in for you.

Why 2B is a ceiling and not a report

Your supplier files their outward statement. The government assembles your GSTR-2B from it on a fixed date each month, and it does not move again. Credit is claimable only to the extent it appears there, so an invoice in your books that your supplier never uploaded is not an asset. It is a receivable from somebody already holding your money.

A business buying 40 lakh a month at 18 percent carries roughly 7.2 lakh of credit that depends entirely on other people's filing discipline. Two suppliers having a bad quarter is a working capital event, and the first symptom is usually a notice long after anything could be done.

We reconcile against 2B and not 2A on purpose. 2A keeps changing as suppliers file late, so it proves nothing about what you could see on the day you decided. Frozen is evidence. Moving is an assertion.

The five categories every row lands in

Nothing sits outside these five, and nothing goes into a general unmatched bucket that mixes two opposite problems together.

CategoryWhat it meansWhat it costs you
MatchedSame GSTIN, same invoice, same period, same taxable value and tax.Nothing. Claim it. On a clean month this is most of the register
In books not in 2BYou hold the bill. Your supplier has not filed it, or filed it against the wrong GSTIN.Your money, today. Most of credit at risk is here
In 2B not in booksThe government has an invoice you have not recorded.Either a bill you lost, which is credit unclaimed, or a document you should refuse
Values differThe invoice matches, the taxable value or the tax does not.Claimable to the lower figure. The gap needs a decision before filing
AmbiguousTwo or more plausible counterparts, usually repeated invoice numbers.Nothing until a person picks. Left to a human on purpose

Confidence scoring, and what a score is for

Real registers do not match on string equality. INV/2024/001 in your books is INV-2024-1 in your supplier's, dated a day apart because one of you booked it on receipt.

  • The score combines GSTIN, invoice number after normalising separators and leading zeros, date within a tolerance, taxable value and tax. None decides alone.
  • A high score sorts your queue. It does not accept the match. Nothing is auto-accepted above a threshold, because a wrong match accepted automatically hides a genuinely missing invoice behind a green tick, and that is the error you will never go looking for.
  • A partial parse of the file is a failure, not a success. A row skipped quietly looks exactly like a supplier who did not file, so you chase an innocent supplier while a deadline runs on credit you were owed.

The two mismatch directions are not the same problem

In books not in 2B is your loss, and it is on a clock. The action is commercial rather than accounting: a named supplier, a named invoice, a call this week, and for repeat offenders a payment term that withholds the tax portion until the credit appears. Section 16(4) eventually closes the window completely — for an invoice from financial year 2024-25, on 30 November 2025 or the annual return, whichever is first.

In 2B not in books splits two ways. Usually it is a bill you never recorded, which is money unclaimed and a purchase your books do not know about. Occasionally it is a supplier who typed a GSTIN wrong and dropped a stranger's invoice into your statement, and claiming it is how you inherit someone else's problem.

Which is why the two are never netted into one unmatched figure. They point in opposite directions and demand opposite actions, and a netted number is arithmetic nobody can act on. It is also what most spreadsheets produce.

What credit at risk means, in rupees

One headline number, and worth knowing how it is built before you take it into a supplier meeting.

  • It is the tax, not the invoice value. A 10 lakh invoice at 18 percent puts 1.8 lakh at risk. It is the tax on rows in books not in 2B, plus the shortfall where values differ.
  • Blocked credit under Section 17(5) is excluded. It was never claimable, so counting it as at risk sends you chasing a supplier over money you could not have had.
  • The figure is aged. Two months at 40,000 is a nuisance. Nine months at 6 lakh with a November deadline is a different meeting.

A month-end, in the order it happens

About three working days for a register in reasonable shape, most of it the chase list rather than the matching.

  1. Import and match

    You download the statement and import the JSON or the Excel. The raw file is stored before it is parsed, because the file is the evidence and parse bugs turn up a year later at a notice.

  2. Work the queue, chase, decide

    Ordered by rupees at risk, not by date: fifty rows worth 3,000 between them wait behind one row worth 4 lakh. The in-books-not-in-2B list goes to suppliers drafted for a person to send, then every row is claimed, held or written off with the decision recorded, a held row carrying its Section 16(4) deadline.

  3. Hand over and lock

    Your CA gets the ITC register in the shape GSTR-3B Table 4 asks for, credit available and credit reversed already separated. They file. The period locks.

Filing is a one-way door

Once a return is filed, a wrong claim is not fixed by editing a line. It is reversed in a later period with interest under Section 50 at 18 percent, running from the original date rather than from the day you noticed. Rule 37 adds a second trap: credit taken on an invoice you have not paid within 180 days must be reversed, which catches disputed bills nobody in the business thinks of as outstanding.

So a period is a boundary and not a label. A reconciliation whose own arithmetic does not balance cannot be marked complete, and a locked period cannot be edited quietly. None of this makes the software the filer. Ordence prepares, matches and evidences. Your CA reviews and files.

Questions people actually ask

Our CA already does this in Excel.

Many do, and at a hundred invoices a month it works. It stops working at volume for three reasons: near-matches get matched by eye, nobody records who decided what, and the workbook is rebuilt monthly so last month's chase list is gone.

Does it connect to the GST portal?

No, and it will not. That means handing your login to a third party and depending on a page layout the government changes without notice. You download the file, we import it.

Send us last month's 2B and your purchase register.

Two files. We will run the match and tell you what your credit at risk actually is, before you have bought anything from us.
